source_title: Carnival Corporation & plc - Form 10-K (Fiscal Year ended November 30, 2020)
publisher_issuer: Carnival Corporation & plc (filed with U.S. SEC, EDGAR CIK 0000815097)
company_context: Carnival is the world's largest cruise company. COVID-19 forced a near-total pause of global cruise operations from March 2020, collapsing revenue while the company continued to burn cash on idle ships, crew, and fixed costs, creating an acute liquidity crisis it survived only through massive capital raises.
macro_context: COVID-19 pandemic; CDC No-Sail Order and global port closures halted cruising, producing an effectively zero-revenue operating environment for much of 2020 while heavy fixed and debt-service costs continued.
evidence_summary: Carnival's fiscal 2020 revenues collapsed to $5,595 million from $20,825 million in 2019 (a ~73% decline) and it posted a net loss of about $10.2 billion. With cruising paused, the company disclosed an expected average monthly cash burn of roughly $650 million. To survive, Carnival raised a wave of capital: a ~$5.75 billion debt raise in April 2020 ($4.0B of 11.5% senior secured notes plus $1.75B convertible notes) and a ~$500 million equity offering (62.5 million shares at $8), followed by additional senior secured term loans in September 2020 (~$1.86 billion plus ~EUR 903 million). These raises allowed it to avoid bankruptcy.

source_backed_metrics.april_2020_debt_raise_usd: approximately 5.75 billion (4.0B 11.5% senior secured notes + 1.75B convertible notes)
source_backed_metrics.september_2020_term_loans: approximately 1.86 billion USD plus approximately 903 million EUR

owner_decision_context: With revenue near zero and a ~$650M monthly burn, management had to choose between rapid, expensive, dilutive and high-coupon capital raising versus risking insolvency; they prioritized survival, accepting high financing costs and dilution to build a multi-billion-dollar cash runway.
action_taken: Raised ~$5.75B of secured and convertible debt and ~$500M of equity in April 2020, added ~$1.86B and ~EUR903M of senior secured term loans in September 2020, and cut operating cash burn, building a multi-billion-dollar liquidity buffer to ride out the no-sail period.
outcome_evidence: Despite a ~73% revenue collapse, a ~$10.2B net loss, and ~$650M/month cash burn, Carnival avoided bankruptcy by raising billions in fresh capital and resumed operations as cruising restarted, confirming a high-revenue-base business pushed into severe-distress-but-survival.

Exact period-end cash balance not separately confirmed and omitted.

In April 2020 Carnival raised approximately $5.75 billion of debt and approximately $500 million of equity

inferred: Carnival was a high-revenue (normally ~$20B) business driven into an acute cash crisis purely by an exogenous demand stop
The willingness to accept expensive secured/convertible debt and equity dilution is what separated survival from bankruptcy
why_useful_for_opsiq: Strong high-revenue-but-cash-crisis case (outcome 7 into 3): a normally ~$20B-revenue company hits a near-zero-revenue, ~$650M/month-burn condition and survives only via emergency capital raises. Tests whether the engine flags the diagnosis as cash/liquidity (not demand-strategy) and treats expensive, dilutive financing as the phase-correct survival action under an exogenous shock.
